title: Isolation scenarios and routing recipes: hosted / dedicated / private
content:
Purpose and audience:
This is an operational sketch for platform engineers and on-call SREs to reason about tenant isolation and request routing across our three serving modes: Hosted API, Dedicated capacity, and Private deployments. It intentionally mixes notes, small config recipes, and decision heuristics — use it as a quick reference when designing a routing change or triaging cross-tenant incidents.

High-level goals (non-exhaustive):
- Preserve tenant isolation guarantees appropriate to mode (data, performance, network).
- Enable predictable routing policies that minimize blast radius under regional failure.
- Provide clear fallbacks and observable signals for automatic and manual remediation.

Core differences summarized:
- Hosted: multi-tenant control plane and shared runtime. Isolation relies on logical fencing (namespaces, request tagging), per-tenant rate limits, and soft-affinity by region. Fastest path for routing changes but weakest in absolute isolation.
- Dedicated: per-tenant GPU pools and isolated runtime clusters. Stronger performance isolation; control plane still central but with explicit tenant-to-cluster binding. Routing must respect capacity reservations and pre-warm state.
- Private: control plane may be split (customer-managed) or shadowed. Network-level isolation (VPC, private links) is primary; routing often controlled by customer or via a lightweight regional agent.

Routing primitives and where they live:
- Edge ingress (global LB): initial geo / latency-based decision. In hosted we own this fully; in private there may be an external front door.
- Tenant tag (X-Redwood-Tenant): authoritative for downstream routing — must be injected or verified at the edge.
- Model variant map: control-plane table mapping tenant+model->serving endpoint (cluster id, model version, quant/profile).
- Capacity affinity token: short-lived token representing reservation on Dedicated clusters to avoid oversubscription during bursty traffic.

Isolation patterns (recipes):
1) Soft-fence (Hosted default):
   - Enforced via per-tenant token buckets, request priority, KV namespace isolation.
   - Routing: edge -> region selector -> model map lookup -> server pool. If pool overloaded, fallback to cheaper model variant or enqueue with small delay.
   - Observability: per-tenant latency, headroom, tail-token-drop rate.

2) Hard-fence (Dedicated):
   - Tenant bound to cluster(s) with reserved GPU quota. Control plane maintains binding and refuses routing to other clusters except explicit failover.
   - Routing: edge -> region -> tenant-cluster binding -> direct VIP to cluster. Use capacity affinity tokens for each request to validate reservation.
   - Failover: warm standby cluster in another region or burst to hosted tier (subject to policy + billing).

3) Network-fence (Private):
   - Routing is typically configured via a customer-managed ingress; our agent exposes a model-map API over private connectivity.
   - For multi-region private, recommend a per-region agent with consistent model-map replication.

Decision heuristics for failover and routing policies:
- Prefer intra-mode failover (dedicated->dedicated) within region first.
- If regional capacity exhausted, try mode-appropriate fallbacks: Dedicated -> Hosted (if tenant allows), Dedicated -> Dedicated in other region, Hosted -> Hosted in other region, Private -> (customer-managed) or alert ops.
- Use policy tags on tenant config: allow-hosted-fallback (bool), max-fallback-latency-ms, billing-fallback (accept/deny).

Control-plane considerations:
- The model-map must be strongly consistent for Dedicated bindings to avoid split-brain (use paxos/raft regionally; replicate bindings asynchronously for hosted performance).
- Use a small TTL for cluster assignments in hosted to allow dynamic packing; Dedicated assignments are longer-lived and require manual or automated rollout workflows.
- Introduce a "routing-intent" log stream for every change (git-style record) and surface in console for on-call.

Observability and SLOs to add to runbooks:
- Per-tenant P95/P99 latency, error rate, and token-drop rate by routing hop.
- Cross-tenant queue length on shared pools (hosted).
- Capacity-affinity miss rate for Dedicated.
- Control-plane stale-binding alerts (binding older than X minutes without refresh).

Playbook snippets (triage):
- If tenant latency spikes and hosted pool CPU saturated: 1) check per-tenant headroom; 2) verify KV cache hit-rate; 3) consider routing to a cheaper variant or enqueueing short window; 4) notify product if frequent.
- If dedicated cluster shows affinity token exhaustion: 1) increase token issuance temporarily (if safe); 2) trigger autoscale/pre-warm; 3) if sustained, initiate cross-region failover per tenant policy.

Config sample (pseudocode):
- tenant config flags:
  allow_hosted_fallback: true
  preferred_regions: ["us-west1","us-east1"]
  max_fallback_latency_ms: 250

Notes / unresolved items to iterate on:
- We need a standard tagging scheme for cross-system tracing (edge -> controlplane -> runtime) to attribute costs more cleanly.
- Policy UI: surface routing-intent and fallback policy in console to reduce on-call confusion during failovers.
- Private multi-region agent upgrade path needs a graceful migration story for model-map schema changes.

Related tickets and references:
- JIRA-PLAT-1094 (routing intent logging)
- RFC: multi-region private agent (link in Confluence: CONFLUENCE-PLT-382)
- PR: routing proto changes (https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing-protos/pull/212)

Next steps:
- Prototype capacity-affinity token in a canary hosted pool and measure miss rate under synthetic burst workload. (Owner: Ethan)
- Draft console UX for fallback policies and routing-intent audit. (Owner: Liu)
- Run a tabletop for Dedicated->Hosted failover with a real tenant and billing guardrails. (Owner: Maya)

Notes to self: keep this doc short and pragmatic — move formal decisions to Confluence once flushed out.
